steps.html:
Icelandic farmers on a Canadian lake. Welsh chapel tea in the Argentinian desert. Two communities that moved eight thousand kilometres and took their festivals with them — and the smallest words in English, which decide how you refer to any of it.

  • Read two accounts of transplanted communities
  • Use a, an, the and no article accurately
  • Talk about customs, ceremonies and settlement
  • Write about a custom or community you know

steps.title: Before you read: what would make you leave your country permanently?
A Viking festival on a Canadian lake
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 144 words

Gimli is a small town on the western shore of Lake Winnipeg, and it has the largest concentration of Icelandic people anywhere outside Iceland. The first settlers arrived in 1875. They were not tourists and they were not explorers; they were farmers whose crops had failed, and they came because a volcano had made the land at home unusable.

Their descendants still hold a festival every August. There is a parade, there are competitions, and a surprising number of citizens of a Canadian province spend a weekend dressed as Vikings.

The costumes are the feature everybody photographs, but the interesting part is quieter. A dialect of Icelandic survived in Gimli for over a century after it had begun to change everywhere else. Linguists came from Reykjavik to record it. The custom that looked like fancy dress turned out to be holding a language open.

steps.title: The Welsh who chose Patagonia
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 147 words

In 1865 a hundred and fifty-three Welsh immigrants landed on an empty beach in southern Argentina. They had been promised farmland. What they found was desert, and the first winter nearly ended the settlement.

It did not end. The community that grew out of that beach is now well established, and around fifty thousand descendants still live in the Chubut valley. They are Argentinian citizens, they speak Spanish all week, and a good number of them also speak Welsh.

The customs travelled with the language. Chapel tea, with bara brith and seven kinds of cake, is still served on a Sunday afternoon. The eisteddfod — a competition in poetry and singing that goes back centuries in Wales — is held every October, in Patagonia, in Welsh.

Globally, most immigrant languages disappear inside three generations. This one did not, and nobody is entirely sure why.

steps.title: a / an, the, and no article at all
steps.html:
You have used these since your first lesson. This is the version that decides B2 accuracy.

Ask two questions in order. First: is the noun countable and singular? If yes, it must have an article — a, the, or a determiner. English does not allow a bare singular countable noun: She is citizen.

Second: can the reader identify which one you mean? If yes, use the. If not, use a / an. They held a festival — you have not met it before. The festival is held every August — now you have.

Use the when the noun is already identified: mentioned before, made specific by what follows (the town on the shore of Lake Winnipeg), or unique (the sun, the government, the first settlers). Superlatives and ordinals always take the.

Use no article for plural or uncountable nouns spoken of in general: Immigrants often keep their customs. Language is what holds a community together. Also for most countries, cities, languages, meals and academic subjects: in Iceland, in Welsh, before lunch.

The traps: the with a general plural. The immigrants often keep their customs means a specific known group. And no article with a singular countable noun. He became citizen — it must be a citizen.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts. Cover the note and say why each article is there.

Gimli is a small town on the western shore of Lake Winnipeg.
A — first mention. The — there is only one western shore.

It has the largest concentration of Icelandic people.
Superlative → always the.

The first settlers arrived in 1875.
Ordinal → the.

They were not tourists and they were not explorers.
Plural, general → no article.

They were farmers whose crops had failed.
Plural, general → no article.

A volcano had made the land at home unusable.
A — new. The — made specific by at home.

There is a parade, and there are competitions.
Singular countable → a. Plural, general → nothing.

The costumes are the feature everybody photographs.
Both already identified by the context.

A dialect of Icelandic survived in Gimli.
First mention of the dialect.

Linguists came from Reykjavik to record it.
Plural, general → no article. City → no article.

They are Argentinian citizens.
Plural after are → no article.

The community that grew out of that beach is now well established.
Made specific by the relative clause that follows it.

steps.title: Choosing an article in four steps
steps.html:
1. The sentence: ___ eisteddfod is ___ competition in ___ poetry and singing.
  2. Gap 1: eisteddfod is singular and countable. Can the reader identify it? Yes — the text has just named it. So the.
  3. Gap 2: competition is singular and countable, and it is new information defining what the eisteddfod is. So a.
  4. Gap 3: poetry and singing are uncountable, spoken of in general. So no article.
  5. Result: The eisteddfod is a competition in poetry and singing. Countable and singular always needs something; general and uncountable usually needs nothing.

steps.title: You are going to write about a custom or a community.

options.label: A festival or ceremony where you live
A community that moved to your country and stayed
A community from your country living somewhere else
A custom in your family that nobody outside it would understand

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Describe it, then say what it is really doing — the way both texts do.
steps.html:
• Say what it is and where.
  • Describe what actually happens, in two or three details.
  • Then say what it is really doing for the people involved.
  • Check every singular countable noun has an article.

Useful language

  • … is a small town / community in …
  • The first settlers arrived in …
  • Their descendants still …
  • The custom that looks like … is in fact …
  • Globally, most … disappear within …
  • Nobody is entirely sure why this one did not.
steps.modelHtml:
Nauryz in a block of flats

Nauryz is a spring festival celebrated across Central Asia, and in my grandmother's village it lasted three days. In the city where I grew up it lasts an afternoon, in a courtyard between four apartment blocks, and it is organised by about six women who have known each other since 1984.

There is a long table. There is nauryz köje, which takes most of the previous day to make. Somebody always brings a speaker and nobody agrees about the music.

The food is the feature everybody photographs. The interesting part is quieter. It is the only day of the year when the whole building stands in the same place at the same time, and the only reason the neighbours on the fourth floor know the neighbours on the first.
